Field notes/ Futures / Field note 02
18 July 2026 / 4 min read

The future used to have a colour.

Written in the voice
of Mara Vey

Original concept essay

There is a particular orange that belongs to old ideas of tomorrow. Not the orange of a warning light, or a sunset, but the softened colour of a book cover left on a windowsill. It suggests a future that was once urgent and has since had time to fade.

I collect these covers for their confidence. Their circles, their impossible buildings, their insistence that an unfamiliar shape could explain an unfamiliar world. They offer no photograph as proof. They ask us to make the journey ourselves.

Tomorrow, handled

What interests me is the distance between the promise and the object. The promised future is weightless. The book is heavy. Its paper yellows, its glue fails, and someone has written a shopping list on the last page. Tomorrow has been handled by ordinary people.

When I imagine a future, I try to give it the same evidence of use. A public terminal with a loose button. A ceremonial building whose roof leaks. A device repaired with a part from a much older device. These details are not there to make the world look charming. They are there to suggest that people have had to live in it.

The marks we leave

A flawless future leaves very little room for a story. A used future carries disagreement in its surfaces. Someone designed this. Someone paid for it. Someone has found a way to make it do something it was never meant to do.

Perhaps that is why the faded orange keeps drawing me back. It contains two times at once: the time of the promise and the time of its survival. The future becomes interesting when it acquires a past.
